amendments.rule: A target head is the cross-language lexical display anchor: the English token that most directly realizes the source head's lexeme, with English syntax used only to break a genuine tie. Choose the lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries (`was gathered` heads on `gathered`), the noun in `of + noun`, and the substantive over a generic English noun supplied to expand it (`living creature` for a substantival adjective heads on `living`; rule 31 gives the test and governs the whole family). Where one morpheme is rendered by a multi-word English preposition, the head is the token carrying the lexeme rather than the connective: `מִן` → *out of* heads on *out*. **Where the ASV recasts one morpheme's relation as a fixed English phrase in which no word realizes that morpheme's own lexeme, head on the content word the phrase turns on, found by rule 31's subtraction test, and never on one of its connectives**: `מִן` → *of one piece with* heads on *piece*, because dropping *piece* leaves the phrase saying nothing while *of*, *one* and *with* are what English spends on the relation, exactly as `מִן` → *by reason of* heads on *reason*. This reaches only a rendering that drops the lexeme; where a word does realize it, the preceding sentence governs and the head stays there. **But a degree word the ASV writes beside a comparative preposition is not the token carrying the lexeme, and the *out of* sentence does not reach it.** Where a comparative `מִן` is rendered by a degree adverb together with the relational word — *more than*, *rather than* — the comparison's own relation is what the morpheme says, and the degree adverb is what English spends on a comparison it writes without one elsewhere, so the unit heads on *than*, exactly as a bare `מִן` → *than* does. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 31 and 43 use: drop *than* and the comparison has no relation left to state, while dropping *more* or *rather* leaves the comparative the ASV writes in that shape throughout. Read which of the two English words the ASV has added rather than which of them stands first, since in *out of* it is the opening word that carries the ablative lexeme and the closing one that is the bare connective, and in *more than* it is the other way about. The corpus aligns `מִן` to *more than* headed on *than* in twenty-five units and to a bare *than* in a hundred and nineteen. Review this choice independently of the unit's edges.
amendments.why: ECC.6 rendered a comparative `מִן` by two English words twice and headed the two units on opposite words: *rather than* on *than* at ECC.6.5, *more than* on *more* at ECC.6.8. Rule 24 as it stood is what produced the disagreement, because its one worked example of a multi-word preposition, `מִן` → *out of* → *out*, has the lexeme in the opening word, and a reader applying it to *more than* reaches *more* and reads *than* as the connective. The amendment names the reverse shape where the rule already implied the answer, and keeps rule 24's own reasoning rather than adding a cross-reference: the corpus aligns `מִן` to *more than* headed on *than* in twenty-five units and to a bare *than* in a hundred and nineteen, with no visible precedent for heading such a pair on the degree word. It is written narrowly, for a comparative preposition rendered by a degree adverb plus the relational word, and does not touch the *of one piece with* or *by reason of* families, which drop the lexeme altogether.

conventions: `מַה־יּוֹתֵר לְ` + noun is written twice in this chapter and is analysed two ways, because the ASV renders it two ways. At ECC.6.8, *what advantage hath the wise* makes the clause possessive, so the `לְ` is what makes it so and carries the *hath* under rule 43. At ECC.6.11, *what is man the better* makes `אָדָם` the English subject and puts the construction-supplied copula on the predicate `יֹתֵר` under rule 20, leaving the `לְ` `unrepresented` under rule 40; giving that `is` to the preposition under rule 49 would leave it holding a word for a relation the English never states. The idiom does not fix the analysis: read the verb the ASV wrote.

The ASV writes *and yet* at ECC.6.6 and ECC.6.7 and the two are aligned differently, because the Hebrew differs: at 6.7 a `גַם` stands in the clause and takes the *yet*, while at 6.6 only the waw stands, it already holds the *and* written for it, and the *yet* is its own `added` unit under rule 51. Reading *though … yet* as a correlative pair on the `אִלּוּ` of 6.6 under rule 14 was considered and set aside, since the ASV's *yet* stands inside the protasis rather than at the head of the main clause, which is *do not all go to one place*. The cross-verse candidate table is keyed by source lemma and so cannot show this pair at all.

report: Read all 30 candidate lemma groups and the full verse dump end to end, the latter because `added` units carry no source token and cannot appear in the candidate table.

One genuine split: a comparative מִן rendered by two English words is headed on *than* at ECC.6.5 (*rather than*) and on *more* at ECC.6.8 (*more than*), with nothing in the source licensing the difference. Patched ECC.6.8 to head on *than*; only the target head moved, and no edge changed.

Basis for that direction: rule 24 heads a multi-word preposition on the token carrying the lexeme, and in a comparative it is the closing *than* that carries the relation while *more* is the degree word English adds. The corpus aligns מִן to *more than* headed on *than* in 25 units and to a bare *than* in 119, and ECC.6.5 already agrees.

Cleared as ASV-licensed rather than split: הַ (unrepresented wherever the ASV writes no determiner; the *the* at 6.7 is rule 29 fronting; the *his* at 6.12 is rule 41's determiner in the article's place, with no suffix in the phrase to claim it); לְ (*hath* at 6.8 verbless possessive, unrepresented at 6.3 where a written הָיָה takes the *have*, at 6.10 as a bare modal complement, at 6.11 where the recasting writes no preposition); לֹא recast as *no* on a nominal at 6.3 and 6.6 alike; and every multi-word substantive head (*untimely birth*, *poor man*, *long ago*, *twice told*), all of which head on the lexeme-bearing word.
*so that* is fused on the waw at 6.2 and split *so* + *that* at 6.3 because שֶׁ stands in the 6.3 clause. That is rule 55's own carve-out, so no convention was recorded for it.

*and yet* is treated two ways: גַם takes the *yet* at 6.7, and it is `added` at 6.6 where only the waw stands and already holds the *and*. Reading *though … yet* as a correlative pair on אִלּוּ was tested and set aside, since the ASV's *yet* stands inside the protasis and not at the head of the main clause. Recorded as a convention, because the candidate table is blind to `added` units.

BSB: none of the 13 disagreements is a genuine error. Six are the documented Td convention difference; the rest are recastings that leave a morpheme with no English at all — the resumptive suffix under *to whom*, the unrendered waw of *riches wealth*, הָיָה absorbing the *have* at 6.3, the bare modal complement at 6.10, and *tell a man* at 6.12 — where BSB attaches the morpheme to its phrase by convention. No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.
One amendment, to rule 24: the case it had not considered is a two-word rendering in which the closing word carries the lexeme, the reverse of *out of*. No new rules.
